question: When should you split off the test set in a project?
options: After feature engineering, so the test set has the final features
First, before exploring the data or making any modeling decision
After choosing the best model
Only if cross-validation is not used
explanation: Any decision informed by the test data biases the final estimate. Splitting first keeps the test set a fair stand-in for future data.

question: In load_breast_cancer, malignant is encoded as 0. Why does that matter when computing recall with sklearn?
options: It does not matter
sklearn treats label 1 as the positive class by default, so recall would measure detection of benign tumors
Recall cannot be computed for label 0
Logistic regression only predicts label 1
explanation: Metrics like recall_score use pos_label=1 by default. Flip the target (or pass pos_label) so the class you care about is positive.

question: Logistic regression, random forest and gradient boosting all score within one standard deviation of each other in CV. Which is a sensible choice?
options: The one with the highest test score
The most complex model, since it can capture more patterns
The simplest model, since the difference is within noise and it is easier to explain and maintain
Average all three test scores
explanation: Differences within CV noise are not evidence of a better model. Prefer simplicity, and never pick using the test set.

question: How should you choose the decision threshold without touching the test set?
options: Always use 0.5
Use out-of-fold probabilities on the training set and pick the threshold that meets the target metric
Try thresholds on the test set and keep the best
Use the predicted probabilities of the training rows from a model fit on all training data
explanation: Out-of-fold predictions come from models that did not see the row, so they behave like held-out predictions. In-sample predictions are overconfident.

question: Lowering the threshold from 0.5 to 0.21 reduced accuracy from 0.974 to 0.895. When is that the right call?
options: Never, accuracy should always be maximized
When missing a positive (false negative) is much more costly than a false alarm, and the lower threshold catches more positives
Only when the dataset is balanced
Only if ROC-AUC also increases
explanation: The threshold encodes the cost trade-off. Trading extra false positives for fewer missed cancers can be correct even though accuracy falls. ROC-AUC does not depend on the threshold.
